Navel
NAY-vel
noun
From the Saxon nafela, the centre or nave of the belly; rendering the Hebrew shor and shorer, the navel or umbilical cord, the mark left in the flesh where a child was once wholly sustained by another.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The navel is the scar of dependence. Every man carries in his own body the plain evidence that he did not make himself, was not self-sustaining, and once received all he had through a cord he did not tie and could not cut. Scripture uses it in exactly that sober register. To the son who keeps wisdom and departs from evil the promise is bodily: “It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones” (Pro 3:8) — the fear of the LORD reaching the frame itself, from the centre outward. Ezekiel draws the harder picture. Israel’s origin was a newborn cast out in the open field: “in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all” (Eze 16:4) — no midwife, no covering, no claim on anyone. And into that helplessness the LORD comes: “when thou wast in thy blood, Live” (Eze 16:6). The covenant does not find a nation attractive; it finds an unwashed infant and speaks life over it. That is unmerited love with the sentiment taken out. The Song can praise the beloved’s body without shame (Son 7:2), because the body is God’s handiwork and the marriage bed is undefiled. The navel therefore says two things at once: you were made, and you were kept, and neither was your doing.

Webster 1828 Definition

The centre of the lower part of the belly, where the umbilical cord was attached; the bodily mark of a creature’s origin and utter early dependence.

expand to see more

NAVEL, n. The centre of the lower part of the abdomen; the point where the umbilical cord of the foetus was attached.

Saxon nafela, from nafa, the nave or centre of a wheel.

Hence figuratively, the middle or central part of any thing.

Hebrew shor, the navel; shorer, the navel-string or cord (Pro 3:8; Eze 16:4).

Used in Scripture of bodily health (Pro 3:8) and of the helplessness of the newborn (Eze 16:4).

Key Scripture

Pro 3:8 — "It shall be health to thy navel, and marrow to thy bones."

Eze 16:4 — "And as for thy nativity, in the day thou wast born thy navel was not cut, neither wast thou washed in water to supple thee; thou wast not salted at all, nor swaddled at all."

Eze 16:6 — "And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live; yea, I said unto thee when thou wast in thy blood, Live."

Son 7:2 — "Thy navel is like a round goblet, which wanteth not liquor: thy belly is like an heap of wheat set about with lilies."

Modern Corruption

Modernity has revived the old gnostic severing of the self from the body — the transgender claim that a man’s embodied sex is incidental to who he really is — against Gen 1:27, Psa 139, and 1Co 6:19–20.

expand to see more

The corruption is ancient wearing new dress. The second-century gnostics taught that the true self is a spark imprisoned in matter and that the body is at best a container and at worst a mistake; the church answered them with the doctrines of creation, incarnation, and bodily resurrection, and the answer has never needed revision. The present form of the error is the claim that a person has a “gender identity” distinct from and authoritative over his body, so that the flesh he was born in may be overruled, medicated, and cut to match an inward sense of self — the very categories “gender assigned at birth” and “gender identity” being the corruption, not merely their misuse. Scripture forecloses it at the first chapter: “male and female created he them” (Gen 1:27), which our Lord treats as settled and sufficient (Mat 19:4). Sex is creational, embodied, and immutable; it is not a costume the self wears, nor a construct the will assigns. The navel is a quiet witness against the whole scheme, for it is the mark of a body received rather than chosen — you were knit together in a womb (Psa 139:13–14), fed by a cord, and delivered into a world you did not consult.

Recover the doctrine that the body is the man, not the man’s property. “Know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body” (1Co 6:19–20). The believer’s flesh is bought, indwelt, and destined for resurrection; it is not raw material. And with the doctrine, recover the pastoral use of Eze 16. The image is deliberately unsparing: an infant in her blood, cord uncut, unwashed, unsalted, unswaddled, exposed in an open field. That is what God’s love found, and He did not find it lovely. He spoke — Live — and it lived. Every soul that is in Christ owes its whole existence to a word spoken over it while it was still repulsive, which is why boasting is excluded and why compassion toward image-bearers caught in this present confusion is a duty, not a concession. Tell them the truth about the body precisely because the body will be raised.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The centre of the belly where the cord was attached; the body’s own record that life was received, not generated.

expand to see more

Navel — Saxon nafela, from nafa, the nave or hub of a wheel; hence a centre.

Hebrew shor (navel) and shorer (navel-string, Eze 16:4).

Pro 3:8 makes the fear of the LORD bodily health, from the centre outward.

Eze 16:4 is the covenant’s origin story: an infant with the cord uncut.

The mark is universal; no man carries it by his own arrangement.

Usage

"Pro 3:8 promises health to the navel — wisdom reaches the frame, not only the mind."

"Eze 16:4 is unmerited love with the sentiment removed: God’s love found nothing lovely."

"The navel answers every claim that the self stands free of the body it was born in."
